title: Questions
description: Ask yes-or-no questions three ways: intonation, est-ce que and inversion.
rule: A yes-or-no question can keep statement order with a rising voice (Tu viens ?), or start with est-ce que, shortened to est-ce qu’ before a vowel sound, still with normal order (Est-ce que tu viens ?). Inversion puts the verb before a subject pronoun, joined by a hyphen (Viens-tu ?); when the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun is il, elle or on, add -t- between them (Parle-t-il ? A-t-elle ?), but not after a verb ending in -t or -d (Finit-il ? Prend-il ?). With a noun subject, keep the noun first and add the matching pronoun after the verb (Paul vient-il ?). In the passé composé, invert only the auxiliary and pronoun, then the participle (As-tu mangé ?). A negative question keeps ne and pas around the verb (Tu ne viens pas ? N’aimes-tu pas le thé ?), and a yes that contradicts it is si, not oui.
example: Tu viens ce soir ? · Est-ce qu’elle aime le thé ? · Paul vient-il avec nous ?
aside: Inversion sounds careful and is common in writing; in everyday speech most people use intonation or est-ce que. When an exercise does not name a form, any of the three is accepted.

alternatives.message: That is valid French using inversion. This exercise asks for est-ce que with tu before parles.
That is a valid question with rising intonation in speech. This exercise asks you to add est-ce que.

exercises.hint: Put the question opening in front. It changes nothing in the words after it.
exercises.feedback: Use the requested question opening, then keep the statement’s subject before its verb.
exercises.explanation: Est-ce que introduces the question without changing the order of tu parles.

exercises.instruction: Build the question using est-ce que.
exercises.hint: The question opening comes first. After it, keep the statement’s order.
exercises.feedback: The question opening comes first. After it, keep the same subject–verb order as the statement.
exercises.explanation: After est-ce que, the statement’s normal subject–verb order stays unchanged.

exercises.instruction: Complete the question with the missing word from est-ce que. Write only that word.
exercises.hint: Listen to the first sound of nous. Does que need to shorten before it?
exercises.feedback: Complete the fixed question opening. The following consonant sound does not require elision.
exercises.explanation: Que stays complete before nous. The subject nous remains before the verb partons.

exercises.instruction: Fix the word order after est-ce que. Keep all the words.
exercises.hint: After est-ce que, use the same order as in a statement.
exercises.feedback: The question opening is already present. Check whether the subject comes before the verb.
exercises.explanation: Est-ce que uses normal subject–verb order. Inversion is a separate question form, not an extra step after est-ce que.

exercises.instruction: Turn this statement into a question using est-ce que, shortened where needed.

alternatives.message: That is valid French using inversion. This exercise asks for est-ce qu’elle followed by aime.
That is a valid question with rising intonation in speech. Here, use the requested est-ce qu’ form.

exercises.hint: Elle begins with a vowel sound, so que becomes qu’.
exercises.feedback: Use the requested question opening and check its elision before the subject’s vowel sound.
exercises.explanation: Que elides before elle. The subject elle still comes before the verb aime.

exercises.instruction: Build the question using the shortened form of est-ce que.
exercises.hint: The tile ending in an apostrophe joins the word right after it. Then use statement order.
exercises.feedback: Join the apostrophe-ending opening to the subject, then keep the verb after the subject.
exercises.explanation: Que becomes qu’ because the next word is ils, which begins with a vowel sound.

exercises.instruction: Fill the blank with que or its shortened form. Write only the missing part, including any apostrophe.
exercises.hint: Il starts with a vowel sound. What happens to que before a vowel?
exercises.feedback: The following pronoun starts with a vowel sound. Include the apostrophe in the shortened form.
exercises.explanation: Que becomes qu’ immediately before il. The apostrophe joins the two without a space.

exercises.instruction: Fix the elision in this question. Keep the other words unchanged.
exercises.hint: Elles starts with a vowel sound. What happens to que before a vowel?
exercises.feedback: The subject–verb order is correct. Check the elision immediately before the subject.
exercises.explanation: Que must elide before elles. The order elles arrivent is already correct.

exercises.instruction: Turn this statement into a question using est-ce que. Keep the noun subject.
answers: Est-ce que le train arrive demain ?

alternatives.message: That is valid French using inversion. This exercise asks you to put est-ce que before le train arrive demain.
That is a valid question with rising intonation in speech. This exercise specifically asks for est-ce que.

exercises.hint: Put Est-ce que before the whole statement. Le train remains before arrive.
exercises.feedback: Keep the complete noun subject before its verb and add the requested opening before both.
exercises.explanation: The same pattern works with a noun subject: est-ce que, then le train, then arrive.

exercises.instruction: Build the question using est-ce que. Keep the noun subject.
answers: Est-ce que la porte est ouverte ?
exercises.hint: After the question opening, keep the words of the statement in their order.
exercises.feedback: The two-word noun subject belongs between the question opening and the verb.
exercises.explanation: Est-ce que adds a question opening; it does not reverse the statement’s subject and verb.

exercises.instruction: Write the missing question opening: est-ce que or its shortened form.
exercises.hint: Look at the sound right after the blank. Does que need to shorten before it?
exercises.feedback: Supply the complete question opening. Its final word is followed by a consonant sound.
exercises.explanation: Que is followed by le, not by café. There is no elision, and le café stays before est.

exercises.instruction: Fix the word order after est-ce que. Keep l’enfant as the subject and keep all the words.
exercises.hint: After est-ce que, the subject comes before the verb, just as in a statement.
exercises.feedback: Keep the noun subject together and place it before the verb, just as in a statement.
exercises.explanation: L’enfant stays together as the subject. Que does not elide here because the next sound is the l in l’enfant.

exercises.instruction: Choose the question that uses rising intonation only.
exercises.source: A casual question to a friend: are you coming tonight?
options: Est-ce que tu viens ce soir ?
exercises.hint: Look for the question whose words are in exactly the same order as a statement, with nothing added.
exercises.feedback: One option adds est-ce que and one swaps the verb and the pronoun. Intonation changes neither.
exercises.explanation: Tu viens ce soir ? is the statement Tu viens ce soir with a rising voice. Viens-tu uses inversion and Est-ce que tu viens adds an opening.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French using rising intonation only.
exercises.source: Do you have a car? (to a friend)

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que tu as une voiture ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question, but here use intonation only, without est-ce que.
That is correct inversion, but here keep tu before the verb and use intonation only.

exercises.hint: Say the statement “you have a car” to a friend and let your voice rise at the end.
exercises.feedback: Keep tu before the verb and add nothing at the start.
exercises.explanation: An intonation question is just the statement Tu as une voiture with a question mark.

exercises.instruction: This question mixes intonation and inversion. Fix it so it uses intonation only.

alternatives.message: That is correct inversion, but here keep vous before the verb and use intonation only.

exercises.hint: An intonation question says the subject only once, before the verb.
exercises.feedback: The subject pronoun appears twice. Keep the one that gives statement order.
exercises.explanation: With intonation, the order is the statement’s: Vous parlez anglais ? The extra -vous belongs only to inversion.

exercises.instruction: Build the casual question using intonation only.
exercises.hint: Use the statement order: subject, verb, then the time.
exercises.feedback: Intonation needs no pronoun after the verb. Leave out the tile that adds one.
exercises.explanation: Ton frère arrive ce soir ? keeps statement order. The tile arrive-il is wrong in any case: inversion here would need -t-.

exercises.instruction: Turn this statement into a question using inversion.

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que vous aimez le fromage ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Put the verb first, then the pronoun, joined by a hyphen.
exercises.feedback: Swap the subject pronoun and the verb and link them with a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Inversion puts aimez before vous and joins them: Aimez-vous le fromage ?

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct inverted form.
exercises.hint: The verb comes first and must match the pronoun that follows it.
exercises.feedback: Check the order of verb and pronoun, and whether the verb form fits that pronoun.
exercises.explanation: Voulez-vous is vouloir in the vous form, inverted. Vous-voulez has the wrong order and voulez does not go with tu.

exercises.instruction: Write aller for tu, inverted with a hyphen.
exercises.hint: Start with the tu form of aller, then the pronoun.
exercises.feedback: Use the present of aller for tu and put tu after it with a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Tu vas becomes Vas-tu in inversion: Vas-tu au cinéma ce soir ?

exercises.instruction: Build the question using inversion.
exercises.source: Do you take the bus in the morning? (to a friend)
exercises.hint: Start with the verb-pronoun tile, then the bus, then the time.
exercises.feedback: Two tiles look alike. Only one has the right tu form of prendre.
exercises.explanation: With tu, prendre is prends, so the inverted form is Prends-tu. Prend is the il/elle form.

exercises.instruction: Fix the inverted question.

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que vous finissez à cinq heures ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question, but here keep the inversion and fix how it is written.

exercises.hint: In inversion, the verb and the pronoun are written as one unit.
exercises.feedback: The order is right. Check how the verb and the pronoun are joined.
exercises.explanation: An inverted verb and pronoun are always linked by a hyphen: Finissez-vous.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French using inversion.

alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Use the vous form of parler and put vous after it.
exercises.feedback: Formal you is vous. Put the verb first and join the pronoun with a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Parlez-vous anglais ? inverts vous parlez. With a language after parler, the article is optional.

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct inverted form.
exercises.hint: The verb a ends in a vowel and il begins with one.
exercises.feedback: French does not let two vowel sounds meet here. Something must go between them.
exercises.explanation: A-t-il adds -t- between the vowel of a and the vowel of il. Each part is joined by a hyphen.

exercises.instruction: Write the missing letter between the verb and the pronoun.
exercises.hint: Parle ends in a vowel and elle begins with one.
exercises.feedback: A single sound links the two vowels. Write just that letter.
exercises.explanation: When a verb ending in a vowel meets il, elle or on, French adds -t-: Parle-t-elle ?

exercises.instruction: Turn this statement into a question using inversion.

alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Put the verb first. Aime ends in a vowel and elle starts with one.
exercises.feedback: After inverting, check whether two vowels meet between the verb and elle.
exercises.explanation: Aime and elle are separated by -t-: Aime-t-elle le jazz ?

exercises.instruction: Fix the inverted question.

alternatives.message: That is a correct question, but here keep the inversion and fix it.

exercises.hint: Look at the last letter of mange and the first letter of il.
exercises.feedback: The order is right, but two vowels meet between the verb and the pronoun.
exercises.explanation: Mange ends in a vowel, so -t- goes before il: Mange-t-il avec nous ?

exercises.instruction: Translate into French using inversion.

alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Invert travaille and il. Think about the two vowels that meet.
exercises.feedback: Put the verb first, then check what goes between travaille and il. “On Saturdays” is le samedi.
exercises.explanation: Travaille ends in a vowel, so inversion adds -t-: Travaille-t-il le samedi ? Le samedi means every Saturday.

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct inverted form.
exercises.hint: Look at the last letter of the verb before you add anything.
exercises.feedback: The extra -t- is only there to separate two vowels. Check whether this verb already ends in t.
exercises.explanation: Finit already ends in t, so no extra -t- is added: Finit-il ? Fini without t is the past participle, not the present.

exercises.instruction: Turn this statement into a question using inversion. Keep Marie as the first word.

alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Keep the noun, then add the pronoun that stands for Marie after the verb.
exercises.feedback: A noun subject is not moved. It is repeated by a pronoun after the verb, and the vowel rule still applies.
exercises.explanation: Marie stays first; elle is added after travaille with -t-: Marie travaille-t-elle ici ?

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct form.
exercises.hint: The pronoun after the verb stands for tes parents, and the verb agrees with it.
exercises.feedback: Check the verb ending and whether a -t- is needed between the verb and ils.
exercises.explanation: Viennent-ils repeats tes parents with ils. Viennent ends in t, so no extra -t- is added.

exercises.instruction: Fix the inversion. Keep Paul as the first word.
exercises.hint: A noun subject does not move after the verb in a yes-or-no question. A pronoun does.
exercises.feedback: Put Paul back before the verb and add the pronoun that stands for him after it.
exercises.explanation: With a noun subject, keep the noun first and add il after the verb: Paul vient-il ce soir ?

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que Paul vient ce soir ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks you to fix the inversion: Paul vient-il ce soir ?
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks you to fix the inversion: Paul vient-il ce soir ?

exercises.instruction: Build the question using inversion with the noun subject.
exercises.source: Does the bus leave at noon?
exercises.hint: Start with le bus, then the verb with the pronoun that stands for it.
exercises.feedback: Two verb tiles look alike. Check whether part needs an extra -t-.
exercises.explanation: Le bus stays first and il is added after part. Part already ends in t, so there is no extra -t-.

exercises.instruction: Write jouer in the present with the inverted pronoun that stands for ta sœur.
exercises.hint: The pronoun for ta sœur is elle, and joue ends in a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Write the verb, a linking letter if two vowels meet, then the pronoun, all with hyphens.
exercises.explanation: Ta sœur is repeated by elle after the verb, with -t- between the vowels: Ta sœur joue-t-elle du piano ?

exercises.instruction: Translate into French using inversion. Start with Léa.

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que Léa aime la mer ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Keep Léa first and repeat her with a pronoun after the verb.
exercises.feedback: Léa stays in front. Check the vowels between aime and the pronoun.
exercises.explanation: Léa is repeated by elle, linked with -t-: Léa aime-t-elle la mer ?

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct form.
exercises.hint: The added pronoun must match ta mère, and habite ends in a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Check two things: the pronoun’s gender and the link between two vowels.
exercises.explanation: Ta mère is feminine, so the pronoun is elle, joined with -t-: habite-t-elle.

exercises.instruction: Turn this statement into a question using inversion.

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que tu as fini ton café ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: In the passé composé, only the auxiliary swaps places with the pronoun.
exercises.feedback: Invert as and tu, and leave the participle after them.
exercises.explanation: The auxiliary as is inverted with tu, and fini follows: As-tu fini ton café ?

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct inverted form.
exercises.hint: Which word is inverted with the pronoun: the auxiliary or the participle?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun joins the auxiliary, and the participle comes after both.
exercises.explanation: As-tu vu inverts the auxiliary as with tu, then adds the participle vu.

exercises.instruction: Write avoir for vous, inverted with a hyphen.
exercises.hint: Invert the auxiliary, not fini.
exercises.feedback: Write the vous form of avoir, then the pronoun, joined by a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Vous avez fini becomes Avez-vous fini ? The participle stays after the pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Build the question using inversion.
exercises.hint: Start with the auxiliary and pronoun, then the participle.
exercises.feedback: Two auxiliary tiles look alike. Check what goes between a and elle.
exercises.explanation: A and elle are separated by -t-: A-t-elle téléphoné à sa mère ?

exercises.instruction: Fix the word order in this inverted question.
exercises.hint: The pronoun attaches to the auxiliary, not to the participle.
exercises.feedback: Move vous next to the auxiliary and put the participle after it.
exercises.explanation: In the passé composé, invert the auxiliary and the pronoun: Avez-vous vu mes clés ?

exercises.instruction: Translate into French using inversion.

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que vous avez bien dormi ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Invert the auxiliary with vous. Short adverbs such as bien go before the participle.
exercises.feedback: Use avoir for vous, invert it, then put bien and dormi after the pronoun.
exercises.explanation: Avez-vous bien dormi ? inverts the auxiliary; bien sits between the pronoun and the participle.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right reply.
exercises.source: — Tu ne viens pas ? — ____, je viens !
exercises.hint: The reply contradicts a negative question.
exercises.feedback: The speaker is coming, which goes against the question. French has a special yes for that.
exercises.explanation: Si is the yes that contradicts a negative question. Oui answers a positive question, and non would mean the person is not coming.

exercises.instruction: Write the one-word reply that contradicts the negative question.
exercises.source: — Vous n’aimez pas le fromage ? — ____, j’adore ça !
exercises.hint: The answer disagrees with a question containing ne…pas.
exercises.feedback: This is a yes, but not the usual one.
exercises.explanation: After a negative question, yes is si: Si, j’adore ça !

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
answers: Est-ce que tu n’as pas faim ?

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne: Tu n’as pas faim ?

exercises.hint: Avoir faim is the French for “to be hungry”. Put the negation around the verb.
exercises.feedback: Use tu with avoir faim and wrap ne…pas around the conjugated verb. Ne becomes n’ before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Tu n’as pas faim ? keeps n’…pas around as. With inversion, the negation wraps the verb and pronoun together: N’as-tu pas faim ?

exercises.instruction: Make this question negative. Keep the inversion.
exercises.hint: The negation wraps around the inverted verb and pronoun as one block.
exercises.feedback: Put ne, shortened before a vowel, before the verb, and pas after the pronoun.
exercises.explanation: In an inverted question, ne goes before aimes-tu and pas after it: N’aimes-tu pas le poisson ?

exercises.instruction: The question was: Il ne travaille pas aujourd’hui ? Fix the reply so it means yes, he is working.
exercises.hint: A yes that answers a negative question is a different word.
exercises.feedback: The rest of the reply is right. Change only the first word.
exercises.explanation: The reply contradicts a negative question, so French uses si instead of oui.
